title: Hannah Arendt

cards.b:
Hannah Arendt (1906–1975) was a German-Jewish thinker who studied with Heidegger and Jaspers. She fled Nazi Germany in 1933, was briefly held in a French camp, and reached the USA in 1941. She was stateless from 1937, when Germany stripped her citizenship, until she became a US citizen in 1951.

Her key works: The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951), The Human Condition (1958), Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963), On Revolution (1963) and On Violence (1970).

UPSC asks about her views on power, freedom and totalitarianism.

Arendt said Nazism and Stalinism were a new form of government, not just harsh tyranny.

  • Its roots lay in antisemitism, imperialism and the breakdown of the class system into lonely, rootless masses.
  • It ruled by ideology and terror. Ideology explained all of history by one idea, such as race or class.
  • Its central institution was the concentration camp, where it tried to make human beings superfluous.
  • Its ground was loneliness: people cut off from each other and from a shared world.

In The Human Condition, she separates three activities:

Labour

What we do to stay alive: eating, cleaning, producing to consume. It leaves nothing lasting.

Work

Making durable things: tables, buildings, art. It builds a human world.

Action

Speaking and acting together with others in public. Only action is truly political, and only it reveals who we are.

She warned that modern society had raised labour and consumption above action.

Action depends on plurality: we are all the same in being human, yet no two people are alike. Politics exists because many different people share one world.

Natality means every birth brings someone new into the world, able to begin something unexpected. This is the root of human freedom.

For Arendt, freedom is not a private choice or free will. It is something we experience in public, when we act together with others.

In On Violence, Arendt rejects the common view that power grows out of force.

  • Power is the human ability to act in concert. It belongs to a group and lasts only as long as the group holds together.
  • Violence is instrumental. It uses tools and can destroy power, but it can never create it.

Where one rules absolutely, the other is absent. A regime that relies on violence has already lost its power.

This directly challenges Mao's line that power grows out of the barrel of a gun.

In 1961, Arendt reported on the trial of Nazi official Adolf Eichmann in Jerusalem for The New Yorker.

She expected a monster. She found a dull bureaucrat who spoke in clichés and seemed unable to think from another's point of view.

She called this the "banality of evil": great evil can be done by ordinary people who simply stop thinking and follow orders. The book caused fierce controversy, especially over her remarks on Jewish councils.

In On Revolution, she praised the American Revolution for founding lasting freedom through a constitution. She said the French Revolution failed because it was swamped by the "social question" of poverty.

She admired councils and town meetings, where ordinary people took part directly.

From her own statelessness, she said the most basic right is "the right to have rights": the right to belong to a political community. Without it, so-called human rights protect no one.

• Her split between the political and the social seems to leave poverty out of politics. Critics say this is unrealistic.
  • Her admiration for the Greek polis ignores that it rested on slaves and excluded women.
  • Feminists such as Adrienne Rich criticised her, while others like Seyla Benhabib rebuilt her ideas.
  • Her essay "Reflections on Little Rock" (1959), which opposed forced school desegregation, drew strong criticism, including from Ralph Ellison.

Arendt worried that modern society had blurred the line between the private and the public.

In ancient Greece, the household dealt with needs: food, work, family. The polis was the space of freedom, where citizens acted as equals.

Modern times brought the social: economic concerns took over public life. Politics became mainly about managing the economy and administering welfare.

Her worry was that this turns citizens into jobholders and consumers. Government becomes housekeeping on a national scale. The space for real action and debate shrinks.

She also warned against bureaucracy, which she called "rule by Nobody". In it, no one can be held responsible, which can be the most tyrannical form of all.

Her idea of power as acting in concert fits the Gandhian non-violent movement: mass non-cooperation made colonial violence powerless.

Her concern with statelessness speaks to debates about the Rohingya refugees and the NRC in Assam, where about 19 lakh people were left out of the final list in 2019.

Her praise of councils echoes India's experiments in grassroots democracy, such as gram sabhas under the 73rd Amendment.

"Explain Arendt's distinction between power and violence."
"Discuss Arendt's concept of action in The Human Condition."
"What did Arendt mean by the banality of evil?"

Structure: her life as context, totalitarianism, labour-work-action, plurality and natality, power vs violence. Use Gandhi as your Indian example of power without violence.

quiz.q: For Arendt, the truly political activity is…
quiz.w: Action, speaking and acting together in public.

o: Control of the means of violence
The ability to act in concert
quiz.w: Power belongs to a group acting together; violence can destroy it but not create it.

quiz.q: 'The banality of evil' comes from her report on the trial of…
Arendt's idea of natality refers to…
o: The human capacity to begin something new
quiz.w: Each birth brings a new beginning: the root of freedom.

quiz.q: Arendt praised which revolution for founding lasting freedom?
quiz.w: She said the American Revolution succeeded where the French was swamped by the social question.

o: The right to belong to a political community
quiz.w: Without membership in a political community, human rights protect no one.
No one can be held responsible.

quiz.q: Which activity in The Human Condition creates durable things?
quiz.w: Work fabricates a lasting human world.

quiz.q: Arendt's report on Eichmann first appeared in…
quiz.w: The New Yorker, 1963, then as a book.

sources: Hannah Arendt, The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951)
Hannah Arendt, Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963); On Revolution (1963); On Violence (1970)
Seyla Benhabib, The Reluctant Modernism of Hannah Arendt (1996)
PYQ themes: power vs violence, action, totalitarianism (Paper I)
